papers.title: Target engagement and efficacy in disease-modifying trials of synuclein-related disorders.
papers.abstract: Disease-modifying trials in Parkinson's disease (PD), multiple system atrophy (MSA), and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) increasingly incorporate fluid and imaging biomarkers to demonstrate target engagement, de-risk subsequent phases of drug development and provide mechanistic evidence of biological activity. Whether biomarker modulation predicts clinical benefit remains unclear. We conducted a PRISMA-compliant review of phase II and III disease-modifying trials (2020-2025) that included at least one biomarker intended to assess target engagement. Twenty-six trials met inclusion criteria (PD=19, MSA=4, DLB=3; n=2,195 participants). Target engagement was reported in 14 of 19 PD trials (12 phase II/2 phase III), 1 of 4 MSA trials, and 2 of 3 DLB trials (all phase II). Concordance between target engagement and clinical improvement was uncommon, as only 8/26 studies (7 phase II/1 phase III) demonstrated both target engagement and statistically significant clinical benefit, and just two of these (both phase II, one in PD and one in MSA) were rigorously controlled with low or moderate risk of bias. Nine trials showed target engagement without clinical benefit, whereas two reported clinical improvement without measurable target engagement. Baseline biomarker-guided patient selection was uncommon and rarely aligned with the compound's mechanism of action. Patient-reported outcomes were widely used but rarely improved. Across recent disease-modifying trials in PD, DLB, and MSA, target engagement was frequently demonstrated, yet clinical benefit rarely followed. These findings question the predictive value of currently used target-engagement biomarkers and highlight the need to biologically align trial populations with the mechanisms targeted by experimental molecular interventions.

papers.title: Lactoferrin-modified MSC-derived extracellular vesicles facilitate BBB penetration and enhance gastrodin-induced neuroprotection in Parkinson's disease: involvement of mitophagy.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) severely impedes neuroprotective agent delivery to the brain in Parkinson's disease (PD). Although gastrodin (Gas) possesses neuroprotective properties, its efficacy is limited by poor BBB permeability. This study aimed to develop a brain-targeted extracellular vesicle (EV) delivery system for Gas and elucidate its neuroprotective mechanisms. METHODS: A brain-targeted EV delivery system was developed using mesenchymal stem cell-derived EVs modified with lactoferrin (Lf). Gas was loaded into Lf-EVs via sonication to construct Lf-EVs-Gas nanocomplexes. The nanocomplexes were characterized by transmission electron microscopy, western blotting, and nano-flow cytometry. Trans RESULTS: Lf-EVs-Gas exhibited a typical cup-shaped morphology, with a mean size of 79.08 nm and a drug loading efficiency of 47.08 ± 4.63%. Lf functionalization significantly enhanced BBB transport, achieving a brain Gas concentration of 10.34 ± 2.7 ng/g in PD mice versus undetectable levels for free Gas. The targeted system demonstrated superior brain accumulation versus non-targeted vesicles. In 6-OHDA-treated SH-SY5Y cells and MPTP-induced PD mice, the system upregulated tyrosine hydroxylase, reduced α-synuclein aggregation, inhibited neuronal apoptosis, and improved motor function. Mechanistically, these protective effects of Lf-EVs-Gas were associated with activation of PINK1-related mitophagy, as evidenced by elevated LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and increased TOMM20/LC3 colocalization. CONCLUSION: Lf-EVs-Gas enhanced the brain delivery of Gas and produced neuroprotective effects in cellular and mouse toxin-based models of PD. These effects were associated with the activation of PINK1-related mitophagy, supporting Lf-modified EVs as a promising brain-targeted delivery platform for Gas. Further studies establishing mechanistic causality, long-term safety, and efficacy in progressive PD models are warranted.

papers.title: Targeting the Gut to Modify Parkinson's Disease: From Mechanisms to Potential Therapeutics.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder and its prevalence continues to rise with population aging. Its cardinal motor features arise from the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, accompanied by intraneuronal α-synuclein aggregates known as Lewy bodies. Neuropathological evidence suggests that, in a subset of patients, α-synuclein pathology first appears in the enteric nervous system and ascends to the brain via the gut-brain axis. Consistent with this "body-first" trajectory, a growing body of work has documented distinct alterations in gut microbial composition and microbiota-derived metabolites in people with PD relative to healthy individuals, with some changes detectable in the prodromal phase. Current management, whether dopaminergic pharmacotherapy or deep brain stimulation, alleviates motor symptoms but does not slow neurodegeneration, and long-term treatment is complicated by motor fluctuations and other adverse effects. Therapies directed at the underlying disease process are therefore urgently needed. Because early perturbations of the gut microenvironment appear to contribute to PD pathogenesis, interventions that restore gut homeostasis represent a rational disease-modifying strategy, particularly for patients whose pathology originates in the gut. This review synthesizes current understanding of how the gut microbiota shapes the gut-brain axis in PD, spanning immune, metabolic, neuroendocrine, and neural pathways, and critically appraises the emerging evidence for microbiota-directed interventions, including fecal microbiota transplantation, probiotics, and prebiotics, as candidate disease-modifying therapies.

papers.title: The link between inflammation and autonomic dysfunction in alpha-synucleinopathies - narrative review.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Alpha-synucleinopathies are a group of disorders characterized by the accumulation of the pathological form of alpha-synuclein. This group comprises Parkinson's disease, Parkinson's disease dementia, multiple system atrophy, dementia with Lewy bodies, pure autonomic failure, and idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder. Despite sharing a similar molecular basis, these disorders differ in their clinical presentation. Characteristic manifestations include signs of autonomic failure such as orthostatic hypotension, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, constipation, gastroparesis, urinary incontinence, and erectile dysfunction, among others. These symptoms significantly impair patients' daily functioning and are also negative prognostic factors. STATE OF THE ART: Currently, research is investigating the link between inflammation and dysautonomic symptoms. Elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, and IFN-α, have been found to accompany these symptoms. Notably, in other diseases characterized by chronic inflammation, autonomic dysfunction is also common. CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS: In two human studies of dysautonomic symptoms in other conditions, intravenous immunoglobulin therapy was shown to improve these symptoms. Animal studies have shown that other immunomodulatory agents reduce symptom severity. FUTURE DIRECTIONS: Modulation of inflammation, dietary modification, the use of probiotics and prebiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation are potential therapeutic approaches for these diseases. These approaches offer hope for improving the quality of life of patients with alpha-synucleinopathies. Further research in this area is needed.

papers.title: Olive leaf-derived exosome-like vesicles attenuate neurotoxicity in an in vitro rotenone model of Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease primarily characterized by dopaminergic neuronal loss, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and protein aggregation. Despite extensive research, current therapeutic options remain limited to symptomatic management, underscoring the need for neuroprotective strategies targeting disease pathology. In this study, we investigated the neuroprotective potential of exosome-like vesicles derived from olive (Olea europaea) leaves (Ole-ELVs) in an in vitro PD model induced by rotenone in SH-SY5Y human neuroblastoma cells. To evaluate the protective impact of olive leaf-derived ELVs, oxidative stress, cell viability, mitochondrial function, and protein aggregation were assessed by measuring reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay, JC-1 mitochondrial membrane potential staining, and Thioflavin S staining for α-synuclein aggregation. Our findings indicate that treatment with Ole-ELVs significantly attenuated rotenone-induced ROS production, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential, and reduced protein aggregation. Collectively, these results suggest that Ole-ELVs exert neuroprotective effects through antioxidative, protection against cytotoxicity, and mitochondrial-stabilizing mechanisms, offering a promising natural nanoscale therapeutic candidate for PD.

papers.title: Caregiver Burden and Its Determinants After Subthalamic Nucleus Deep Brain Stimulation for Parkinson's Disease: A Cross-Sectional Long-Term Follow-Up Study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, leading to increasing functional dependence even after deep brain stimulation (DBS). Although DBS improves motor outcomes, its long-term impact on caregiver burden remains poorly understood. OBJECTIVES: Our aims were to evaluate caregiver burden after subthalamic nucleus (STN)-DBS and identify patient- and caregiver-related factors associated with burden across different postoperative time points. METHODS: A cross-sectional study of caregivers of PD patients who underwent STN-DBS at a tertiary center, stratified by time since surgery (2-3, 5-6, 10-11, and ≥15 years), was conducted. Caregivers completed the Zarit Burden Interview, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, and an investigator-developed questionnaire. Patient clinical data, including the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS), Part III, scores, were obtained from medical records. Group comparisons and multivariable regression analyses were performed to identify factors associated with caregiver burden. RESULTS: Eighty-eight patient-caregiver pairs were included. Caregivers were predominantly female (62.5%), with a mean age of 60.0 ± 12.3 years. Caregiver burden was mild to moderate but increased independently with longer time postsurgery. Higher burden was associated with younger caregiver age, higher anxiety and depression scores, greater caregiving time, less personal time, and patient-related factors, including dysphagia, dementia, and male sex. Motor severity (UPDRS III, falls, postural instability) was not associated with caregiver burden. Most caregivers considered STN-DBS beneficial and would choose surgery again. CONCLUSIONS: Caregiver burden increased with longer time after STN-DBS and was associated with dementia, dysphagia, and caregiver-related factors but not with motor severity. papers.title: Gesture-based rehabilitation as an assistive technology for post-infectious and post-critical illness disabilities: opportunities and challenges.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This commentary examines gesture-based rehabilitation (GBR) as an assistive technology within an ecosystem for survivors of infectious diseases with neurological disabilities. It describes the roles of computer vision, markerless motion capture, depth cameras, artificial intelligence-driven pose estimation, wearable sensors, smartphone-based tracking, and virtual or augmented reality, while considering infection control and global accessibility. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This commentary was developed by synthesising the existing literature, with an emphasis on camera-based motion capture, gesture-controlled serious games, AI-driven pose estimation, wearable movement sensors, smartphone tracking, and virtual or augmented reality rehabilitation systems. The analysis compares outcomes from traditional neurological conditions, such as stroke and Parkinson's disease, to the specific needs of infectious disease survivors. RESULTS: Evidence from stroke, Parkinson's disease, and other neurological populations suggests that gesture-based systems may support motor rehabilitation, patient engagement, and remote monitoring. GBR may also reduce the need for direct patient-therapist interaction. However, there is currently insufficient direct evidence on the effectiveness, safety, and feasibility of these systems among survivors of infectious diseases. Additional barriers include hardware costs, limited digital infrastructure, and unequal access in rural and resource-constrained settings. CONCLUSION: GBR offers a versatile method for aiding recovery after infectious neurological illnesses. Nonetheless, its safety, effectiveness, and practicality in these groups remain uncertain, as most evidence comes from non-infectious neurological conditions. Specific studies on these populations are necessary before routinely recommending these technologies, along with strategies to overcome technological, financial, and access-related challenges.

papers.title: Disease Duration Differentiates Freezing of Gait Response to Subthalamic and Nigral Stimulation for Parkinson's Disease in an Exploratory Multicenter Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Freezing of gait (FoG) belongs to most pressing unmet symptoms in the treatment of Parkinson's disease. OBJECTIVES: To explore whether combined subthalamic and nigral (STN + SNr) deep brain stimulation improves FoG compared with optimized STN stimulation alone; to identify clinical variables associated with therapeutic response. METHODS: In this exploratory multicenter randomized controlled double-blind trial, we recruited patients from our existing cohorts and randomized them 1:1 to STN or STN + SNr. After baseline, patients were followed with close interim visits (visits 1-5) for 90 days (visit 6). The Freezing of Gait Assessment Course (FoG-AC) was the primary endpoint and was evaluated at P < 0.2 with exploratory intent. Secondary endpoints assessed responder rates, treatment dynamics, predictors of response, and patient preferences. RESULTS: At V6, STN (n = 23) and STN + SNr (n = 22) FoG-AC outcomes did not differ significantly. We identified responders with clinically meaningful FoG improvement in both the STN (n = 7) and STN + SNr (n = 8) groups. In STN + SNr responders, mean disease duration was ~12 years, which was ~4.5 years shorter than in non-responders, but there were no differences in motor and cognitive functions. Treatment dynamics suggested that FoG responders improved slowly and gradually. The STN + SNr responder group showed numerically stronger FoG improvement compared with STN responders. Additionally, 15 STN compared to 10 STN + SNr patients wished to change treatment after the RCT phase and before unblinding. Both STN and STN + SNr treatment was safe. CONCLUSIONS: Future trials evaluating adjunctive STN + SNr stimulation should stratify patients by disease duration to optimize outcomes.

papers.title: Candidate neurobiological pathways linking physical exercise to cognition in Parkinson's disease: a hypothesis-generating translational framework.
papers.abstract: Cognitive impairment is a major nonmotor symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet effective strategies for preserving cognitive function remain limited. Although physical exercise may confer cognitive benefits, the biological pathways linking exercise to cognition in PD remain incompletely established. This narrative review presents a hypothesis-generating translational framework for 4 candidate mechanistic domains that may contribute to exercise-related cognitive effects in PD. First, exercise-responsive neurotrophic signaling, particularly through brain-derived neurotrophic factor-tropomyosin receptor kinase B, insulin-like growth factor 1, and vascular endothelial growth factor pathways, may support synaptic plasticity, neuronal survival, and neurovascular function. Second, exercise may modulate dopaminergic, cholinergic, and noradrenergic systems and influence corticostriatal plasticity relevant to cognitive function. Third, muscle-derived factors and exercise-induced metabolites may affect neurotrophic signaling, neuronal metabolism, and autophagy-lysosomal clearance of α-synuclein. Fourth, exercise may regulate systemic and central inflammatory responses through cytokine signaling, glial activation, inflammasome pathways, and complement-mediated synaptic remodeling. The evidence supporting these pathways is derived from basic, preclinical, observational, and exercise-intervention studies, but the strength of evidence varies considerably across stages of translation. Direct evidence that exercise-induced biological changes mediate cognitive improvement in patients with PD is lacking. These pathways should therefore be regarded as candidate mechanisms for hypothesis-driven investigation of the cognitive effects of exercise in PD.

papers.title: Persistent Therapeutic Burden after Device-Aided Therapy in Parkinson's Disease: Insights from Post-DAT MANAGE-PD Assessment.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Device-aided therapies (DAT) improve advanced Parkinson's disease (PD), but residual therapeutic burden may persist. OBJECTIVES: To explore MANAGE-PD as a framework for characterizing residual disease burden after DAT. METHODS: In this multicenter cross-sectional study, 77 DAT-treated patients underwent independent MANAGE-PD assessment. Clinical characteristics, MANAGE-PD domains, clinician recommendations, and factors associated with Category 3 were analyzed. RESULTS: Of 69 evaluable patients, 38 (55.1%) fulfilled Category 3 criteria, but only three (3.9%) were recommended for an additional DAT. Category 3 patients had more advanced disease, greater non-motor burden, poorer quality of life, and higher oral LEDD (907 vs. 450 mg/day). Freezing/gait impairment, painful dystonia, hallucinations, impulse-control disorders, and persistent OFF periods were major contributors. Only Hoehn and Yahr stage and residual oral LEDD remained independently associated with Category 3. CONCLUSIONS: Persistent therapeutic burden remains common despite DAT. MANAGE-PD may provide a framework for structured post-DAT reassessment.

papers.title: Neuroimmune Dynamics of the Microglia-astrocyte Axis: Implications for Neurodegenerative Disorders as a Double-edged Sword.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Maintaining homeostasis in the Central Nervous System (CNS) requires constant, bidirectional molecular interactions between microglia and astrocytes. This intercellular communication, mediated by cytokines, extracellular vesicles, purinergic signals, and connexin hemichannels, synchronizes immune surveillance, neurogenesis, and synaptic pruning under physiological conditions. However, this interaction can drive persistent neuroinflammation in chronic Neurodegenerative Disorders (NDDs) such as Multiple Sclerosis (MS), Parkinson's Disease (PD), and Alzheimer's Disease (AD). METHODS: Gene disease association analyses and review of existing literature were employed to identify shared glial regulators and molecular mediators across multiple neurodegenerative disorders, supported by schematic diagrams illustrating intercellular signaling dynamics Results: Deregulated astrocytes sustain microglial activation, creating self-amplifying inflammatory loops, while activated M1 microglia induce the conversion of astrocytes into neurotoxic A1 astrocytes via factors such as IL-1α, TNF-α, and complement C1q. Important mediators, such as prostaglandins, IL-1β, and IL-18, further contribute to demyelination, astrogliosis, and excitotoxicity. A convergent glial activation axis identifies shared regulators across several neurodegenerative disorders, including TREM2, GRN, LRRK2, and BDNF. DISCUSSION: Active research targeting reactive astrogliosis and microglial reprogramming towards homeostatic phenotypes shows therapeutic promise. Nevertheless, CNS immune complexity, translational challenge, and inter-patient immunological variability underscore the need for individualized, combinatorial therapeutic strategies and human-relevant experimental models.
